source.excerpt: The miracle is not to walk on water. The miracle is to walk on the green earth in the present moment, to appreciate the peace and beauty that are available now.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section gives the full sentence and cites Touching Peace (1992), p. 1, Parallax Press, ISBN 0-938077-57-0.

We checked that the cited edition is real and correctly described: the Internet Archive’s catalogue record for Touching peace: practicing the art of mindful living gives Parallax Press, Berkeley, 1992, ISBN 0938077570 — the same publisher, year and ISBN.
What we could not do: the Archive’s scan is a lending copy, so we were unable to open page 1 and read the line in the book itself. The page locator here is Wikiquote’s, not our own.
Nhat Hanh wrote and published in English as well as Vietnamese, so no translator stands between this wording and its author — see his biography.
source.excerptNote: The full sentence, as given in Wikiquote’s sourced section with the page citation. Most reproductions cut it after “present moment,” which turns a sentence about appreciating what is already here into a shorter aphorism about walking.

author.metaLine: 1926–2022 · Vietnamese Zen monk, peace activist and author
author.bio: Thích Nhất Hạnh (born Nguyễn Xuân Bảo, 1926–2022) was a Vietnamese Thiền (Zen) Buddhist monk, poet and peace activist, and one of the most widely read Buddhist authors in English. In the mid-1960s he co-founded the School of Youth for Social Services and created the Order of Interbeing; he was exiled from South Vietnam in 1966 after expressing opposition to the war and refusing to take sides, and Martin Luther King Jr. nominated him for the Nobel Peace Prize the following year. In 1982 he co-founded the Plum Village monastery in the Dordogne with the nun Chân Không, and in 1986 co-founded Parallax Press in Berkeley with Arnie Kotler.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right. What travels badly is the sentence itself.

items.who: The shortened version ending at “present moment”
items.why: Nhat Hanh’s sentence ends “… to appreciate the peace and beauty that are available now,” per Wikiquote’s sourced text. The clipped form is not wrong about who said it, only incomplete.

items.who: Quotation sites that give no book at all
items.why: The line is usually reproduced bare, with no book named. It has a precise home — page one of Touching Peace (1992) — and citing it costs nothing. Nobody is falsely credited here; the attribution itself is sound.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Thich Nhat Hanh, opening Touching Peace (1992).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line turns a Gospel scene inside out. Walking on water is Christianity’s shorthand for a miracle that suspends nature; this sentence answers that the real miracle is the thing nature is already doing, and that you are already standing on.

Nhat Hanh had been writing in English for Western readers for years by 1992 — a Vietnamese monk exiled from South Vietnam since 1966, who would go on to devote a whole book to reading Buddha and Christ alongside each other. Placing this sentence on page one of Touching Peace set the terms for everything that followed it.
detailsBody: The truncation matters more than it looks. “Walk on the green earth in the present moment” sounds like an instruction about mindfulness. The clause that follows — “to appreciate the peace and beauty that are available now” — tells you what the walking is for. Cutting it leaves the technique and removes the purpose.

Nhat Hanh co-founded the Plum Village monastery in the Dordogne, in southern France, in 1982 with the nun Chân Không, and in 1986 co-founded Parallax Press — this book’s publisher — in Berkeley with Arnie Kotler. The books of this period were written to be practised from rather than studied.
context.pull: The miracle is not the suspension of the ordinary. It is noticing it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section gives 'The miracle is not to walk on water. The miracle is to walk on the green earth in the present moment, to appreciate the peace and beauty that are available now.' cited to Touching Peace (1992), p. 1, Parallax Press, ISBN 0-938077-57-0. It also gives his dates as 11 October 1926 - 22 January 2022 and describes him as an expatriate Vietnamese Buddhist monk, peace activist and prolific author in Vietnamese and English.

The Internet Archive holds 'Touching peace: practicing the art of mindful living', Berkeley, Calif.: Parallax Press, 1992, ISBN 0938077570 / 9780938077572 - confirming the edition Wikiquote cites. The item is access-restricted (lending), so the page text could not be read.
Thich Nhat Hanh (1926-2022) was a Vietnamese Zen Buddhist monk, author and peace activist.
Plum Village Monastery is a Buddhist monastery in the Dordogne, southern France near Bordeaux, founded by Thich Nhat Hanh and the nun Chan Khong in 1982.
Parallax Press is a non-profit book publisher headquartered in Berkeley, California, founded in 1986 by Thich Nhat Hanh and Arnie Kotler.

Thich Nhat Hanh was exiled from South Vietnam in 1966 after expressing opposition to the war and refusing to take sides; in the mid-1960s he co-founded the School of Youth for Social Services and created the Order of Interbeing; Martin Luther King Jr. nominated him for a Nobel Peace Prize in 1967.
Engaged Buddhism is a Buddhist social movement that emerged in Asia in the 20th century; the article does NOT credit the term to any individual, so no coinage is claimed on this page.
